# Sync and async, side by side

![](../images/spot-1.svg){.spot fig-alt="A small isometric town on a yellow tile, joined to a blue-topped Postgres cylinder by two pipes. An elephant in a hoodie works on a laptop in front."}
SQLAlchemy 2.0 runs the same models and statements in sync and async code, and what async buys is
overlap. Ten queries that each spend 200 ms on the server take about 2 s one after another, and
about 200 ms under `asyncio.gather`, while each query on its own runs no faster. The price is a
lazy-loading error that sync code never raises, and a server connection for every query in flight.

## Drivers and engines

psycopg 3 implements both the blocking and the asyncio interfaces, so one `DATABASE_URL` can serve a
sync engine for scripts and migrations and an async engine for the web app:

```python
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine

url = "postgresql+psycopg://app:pwd@localhost:5432/app"
engine = create_engine(url)              # scripts, Alembic, pandas
async_engine = create_async_engine(url)  # FastAPI
```

With `postgresql+asyncpg://` only the async engine would work, and with `psycopg2` only the sync
one, which is why the lab uses psycopg by default. Most of the code is the same in both styles:

| | sync | async |
|---|---|---|
| engine | `create_engine(url)` | `create_async_engine(url)` |
| connection and transaction | `with engine.connect()` / `engine.begin()` | `async with engine.connect()` / `engine.begin()` |
| session | `Session(engine)`, `sessionmaker` | `AsyncSession(engine)`, `async_sessionmaker` |
| a round trip to the database | a plain call | `await` |
| `select`, `insert`, `text`, models | identical | identical |
| lazy loading | works | raises |

Only the round trip is awaited. `await conn.execute(...)` fetches the rows, and `.one()`, `.all()`
or `.scalars()` afterwards read them from memory.

## Lazy loading in async code

Touching a relationship that has not been loaded makes SQLAlchemy fire a query, and in
`author.notes` there is nowhere to put the `await`. Rather than block the event loop, the async
session raises:

```python
author = (await session.execute(select(Author))).scalars().first()
author.notes   # MissingGreenlet: greenlet_spawn has not been called
```

Attributes that `commit()` has expired fail the same way, which is why `AsyncSession` is almost
always created with `expire_on_commit=False`. The best way out is to eager-load what you need with
`selectinload(Author.notes)`. Failing that, load it explicitly with
`await session.refresh(author, ["notes"])`, or add `AsyncAttrs` to the model and write
`await author.awaitable_attrs.notes`.

## Pool size and concurrency {#what-async-buys-overlapping-waits}

Overlap needs a connection for each query in flight. `create_async_engine` defaults to
`pool_size=5` and `max_overflow=10`, which lets 15 queries overlap while the 16th waits for a free
connection. A thread pool gets the same overlap at the price of one thread per query. Either way the
database does the same total work and only the client stops idling, so when the bottleneck is the
database's CPU, async changes nothing.

## A timed run {#watching-it-happen}

The lab's app answers questions about the SQLAlchemy documentation with pgvector, and its
`POST /trace` endpoint answers the same questions twice with tracing on. The sync run takes them one
after another on one connection, and the async run gives each question its own task and connection
under `gather`. The scene replays one such pair on a shared clock.

::: {.viz .scene .column-body-outset data-src="../viz/index.html?embed=1" data-poster="../images/city.gif" data-title="Vector search with pgvector, sync and async"}
:::
::: {.viz-caption .column-body-outset}
Six questions, sync on the left and async on the right. Each question drops into Python (embedding
with `bge-small`), crosses to its Postgres backend, and lights its five matching chunks in the
documentation field as the HNSW walk returns. Run it live to orbit the scene, or press Replay inside it.
[Open full screen](../viz/index.html){target="_blank"}.
:::

The async plate finishes while the sync one is still working through its queue, and the wall times
in the corner show by how much. Each backend on the async plate is a separate Postgres process, so
the concurrency gained on the client is paid for in connections on the server. Managing that cost is
what [PgBouncer](pgbouncer.qmd) is for.

## Sync libraries inside async code

pandas, Alembic and much older code want a sync connection. `run_sync` hands them one bridged onto
the async connection, so a second engine is not needed:

```python
async with async_engine.connect() as conn:
    df = await conn.run_sync(lambda c: pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM events", c))
```

## Choosing sync or async

Use sync for scripts, notebooks, batch jobs and migrations, where every library works and stack
traces are simpler. Use async for web services and for anything that waits on many databases or
APIs at once, with eager loading, `expire_on_commit=False` and a pool sized for your concurrency. A
mixed code base needs only one driver (psycopg 3), one URL and both engines, with `run_sync` where
the two meet.

::: {.callout-note}
## In the lab

`src/db.py` is the async side of that setup. `src/settings.py` checks every server URL with
pydantic-settings, so a malformed URL fails at import time, before the first query runs.
:::
